page: Amazon Web Services m7i.large is a general-purpose virtual machine instance powered by the AWS Nitro hypervisor. It features an x86_64 architecture with an Intel Xeon 8488C processor operating at 3.2 GHz. The instance is configured with 2 vCPUs derived from 1 physical core with hyper-threading enabled, providing dedicated CPU allocation. Memory resources consist of 8.0 GB of DDR5 RAM operating at 5 GHz, yielding 4.0 GB of memory per core. This instance does not include local storage or GPU accelerators, and it provides a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps.

The underlying Intel Xeon processor supports advanced instruction sets, including Intel Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX, AVX-512) and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX_TILE, AMX_INT8) for matrix math acceleration. Cryptographic operations are accelerated via AES, VAES, and SHA_NI flags. The processor cache configuration includes 48 KB of L1 data cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and 105 MB of L3 cache.

Benchmark results indicate average single-core performance, with a stress-ng single-core CPU score of 1845.29 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1747.0. However, multi-core and memory-intensive benchmarks show limitations due to the 2-vCPU configuration. The stress-ng multi-core performance is rated as poor at 1895.08, and the Geekbench multi-core score is weak at 2133.0. Memory bandwidth benchmarks are also low, with read-only large block bandwidth at 13.5 GB/sec and write large block bandwidth at 14.89 GB/sec. Database operations and Redis SET performance are similarly constrained, with Redis achieving 2.6 million operations per second.

Given its dedicated CPU allocation and DDR5 memory, the m7i.large offers a stable entry-level general-purpose profile. It is suitable for workloads that require consistent single-threaded CPU performance but do not demand high memory bandwidth or multi-core scaling, such as light web serving, text processing, and basic single-threaded utility scripts. The lack of local storage and low baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps represent tradeoffs for data-intensive or high-throughput applications.
